sources.title: The Best Deals Today: Cyberpunk 2077 for Switch 2, Pikmin 4, Star Wars Zero Company, and More
sources.text: A new weekend has arrived, and today, you can save big on Pikmin 4, Cyberpunk 2077 for Switch 2, Doom: The Dark Ages, Star Wars Zero Company, and more. Check out our top picks for Saturday, October 17, below. Walmart has digital copies of Pikmin 4 for Nintendo Switch on sale for $39.88 today. This is just in time before next month's release of Pikmin 4 – Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy. If you grab a copy today, you'll be able to score the Switch 2 upgrade pack for $9.99. That beats paying $70 for a copy any day. Today, you can score a physical copy of Cyberpunk 2077: Ultimate Edition for Switch 2 for $53.42, which is a 365 day low for the platform. This version of the game packs in both Cyberpunk 2077 and the Phantom Liberty expansion. To date, I find this to still be one of the best third party ports for the Switch 2, and it's all on cart! Fanatical has Doom: The Dark Ages - Premium Edition on sale today for $31.49. This edition packs in the base game, this Summer's Revelations DLC , and a few other bonuses, too. If you have not had a chance to check out id Software's latest, it's hard to beat this deal. The Revelations DLC is a great time. Star Wars Zero Company is one of the biggest sleeper hits of the year, and you can save $12 off a physical copy today at Amazon. In our 9/10 review , we wrote, "Star Wars Zero Company is an excellent tactical game that does a fantastic job of slathering on the same cinematic look and feel we saw in Respawn's Star Wars Jedi games, incorporating strong characters and a storyline that's refreshingly centered on non-Force users and a non-traditional villain." If you've been looking for a fantastic new 4K Blu-ray to add to your collection, look no further than 007 The Daniel Craig Collection. You're getting Casino Royale, Quantum of Solace, Skyfall, and Spectre all for $30.81. The unrated and extended version of Casino Royale is even included. Dragon Quest I & II HD-2D Remake is a very ambitious pair of remakes, breathing new life into these classics. Dragon Quest II especially saw huge additions to its story, making this the definitive version of the game. Amazon has PS5 copies for $30, which is the best price we've seen since release. Trails in the Sky 1st Chapter is the first entry in the beloved Trails series, and last year's remake brought new life to the original game. With 2nd Chapter out now, today is a great time to dive into this wonderful RPG series. Similar to previous Nintendo Switch 2 physical releases, Amazon has The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time available for $59.99 right now. This deal will end on release date, which is quickly approaching with us now in October. If you've yet to experience this masterpiece or are diving back into Hyrule, the Ocarina of Time remake is sure to be one of the most talked-about games of 2026. Noah Hunter is a freelance writer and reviewer covering games and technology. When he's not writing for IGN, he runs Final Weapon, a site focused on Japanese games and anime. His favorite series include Xeno, Fate, Final Fantasy, and far too many RPGs to list.

sources.title: Star Wars Zero Company Finally Makes Starting A New Campaign Worth It
sources.text: There has never been a better time to play Star Wars Zero Company I've been waiting for a reason to start a new playthrough of Star Wars Zero Company ever since I beat the game in early September. EA and Bit Reactor have finally given me a reason to come back to the game, as Patch 1.2 added a lot of new gameplay settings that will allow me to tweak my next playthrough's difficulty to my liking. Star Wars Zero Company was an excellent XCOM-like tactics game, but there wasn't much else to mess around with after beating the game once. Players had to turn to mods for more detailed campaign settings, as post-launch updates were nearly nonexistent after Bit Reactor furloughed many developers before release. Bit Reactor brought back some furloughed workers earlier this month and subsequently released Patch 1.2, which goes beyond simple bug fixes. The update includes gameplay tweaks to encourage Upgrade Facility use and make Cly's Combat Jump movement ability less overpowered. The most exciting additions are a plethora of campaign modifiers that let players tweak a campaign's difficulty. Keep in mind that you do have to turn these settings on before you start a new playthrough; they currently can't be changed mid-campaign. It's typically pretty hard for units to die in Zero Company , as they had to be injured three times in one mission. It's now officially possible to turn on "Instant Death" so units die after one injury, or "Two Strikes" so they die after two injuries. Alternatively, players sticking with the three-injury setup can enable a static or escalating "risk of death," which adds a chance that units die when injured. You can also remove or disable health increases from earning Focus Points, disable cross-training for disliked pairs, or reduce the advantage gained from different attack types. Perhaps my favorite new setting is "No Perfect Shots," which adds to the chaos by making it so the maximum chance to hit for any attack is 99%. All these new settings can make Star Wars Zero Company much harder, even on its standard difficulty, and are exactly the kind of modifiers that can draw me back to replay a tactics game. I'm definitely looking forward to a playthrough with the Instant Death and No Perfect Shots settings turned on in the near future. Star Wars Zero Company Update 1.2 is live now across PlayStation 5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X. Bit Reactor also teased that it plans to "explore additional configurations in future updates" for campaign modifiers. If you want to read through the whole list of patch notes in more detail to learn more about every single campaign setting you can now tweak, character nerfs and buffs, and bug fixes, this is what EA and Bit Reactor shared, sans developer notes: The Call For Backup ability can now be bound to a hotkey of your choice.

sources.title: Dragon Quest Monsters: The Withered World details online content, offline Battle Arena, and Wrangler’s Gauntlet
sources.text: Publisher and developer Square Enix , and developer TOSE have released new information and screenshots for Dragon Quest Monsters: The Withered World introducing online content, the offline Battle Arena, and the new roguelike mode Wrangler’s Gauntlet. ■ Team Up With Wranglers the World Over and Take on Joint Battles Together! After you progress some way through the story of Dragon Quest Monsters: The Withered World , you’ll unlock a host of online content. These modes are enabled for cross-platform play, meaning you can enjoy them with anyone, regardless of their chosen gaming system. One of those modes is Online Joint Battles, where you can team up with other wranglers to test your skills against massive monsters together. There are daily quests to try your hand at, as well as special events featuring infamous monsters from across the Dragon Quest series, with fantastic rewards for those able to overcome the challenge! —With three difficulties of regular quests to choose from, you can select the level of challenge that best matches your current party’s strength. —Once you’ve chosen the quest you want to take on, you can start the matching process to find other players. You can also choose to play alone if you wish. —During battle, you can talk with your teammates using a selection of simple preset messages—and you’ll need to communicate if you want to emerge victorious! —When you use healing and support skills on allied parties in battle, you’ll boost your collective Team Bonus. This multiplier increases the damage that everyone can inflict on the enemy and boosts the effectiveness of healing abilities. —Keep an eye out for super-tough Special Quests that feature special monsters. These events regularly come and go, so be sure to give them a try if you’re feeling strong enough. You can earn monster eggs as rewards for completing Online Joint Battles and other challenges. The monsters that hatch forth can then be added to your party! —Eggs come in four colors, and all sorts of monsters can be inside. ■ Connect Online to Access a Wealth of Extra Content! In addition to Online Joint Battles, connecting online allows you to battle against other players in Ranked Matches to improve your global ranking, fight parties that players have uploaded via the Wranglers Society and much more. However, because the online content, such as Online Joint Battles and Ranked Matches, is intended to be a fair test of your monster wrangling skills, the Wrangler’s Spirit ability won’t activate in these game modes. —In Ranked Matches, you compete against other players of a similar ability to yours. There are seven main ranks, from Beginner to Legendary, and the goal is to rise as far you can in the standings. —Every victory rewards you with Ranking Points. Your total at the end of a season determines your rank. Perform well and you might earn promotion to a higher rank, with rewards for doing so! —In Private Matches, you can customize the rules of battle, such as setting the number of rounds or the times you can swap in your reserves. —Head over to the Online Hub, where other players are represented, to participate in the Wranglers Society. By speaking to the wranglers there, you can battle against their parties, so be sure to take your strongest monsters along with you. —Win a battle in the Wranglers Society and you’ll get to spin the roulette wheel to determine your reward, with items, mini medals and other great prizes up for grabs. —The Online Shop has some valuable items for sale. The lineup changes depending on the day of the week and your progress through the story, so check back regularly to see what new stock has come in. ■ The Battle Arena, Where Monster Wranglers Go to Test Their Mettle! In addition to the online content, there’s also a fully offline Battle Arena to enjoy, which Bianca and Nera will discover upon visiting Witherwood Castle. In these contests, you’ll send the monsters you’ve raised into battles that will determine the strongest wrangler in the kingdom. This Battle Arena features both regular battles and joint battles, each with seven difficulty categories from G up to A. With rewards on offer for completing a category, the Battle Arena is the perfect place to test your skills or take a break from adventuring. —In the regular Arena Battles, you have to win all three matches in a category to complete it. Your monsters’ HP and MP will be fully restored between matches, so you can always fight to the max. Once you pay the entry fee, it’s time to start battling! —During battle, you can choose the general tactics you want your monsters to follow. Keep close tabs on how each battle plays out and adjust your tactics accordingly. —In Joint Battles at the arena, you can set the tactics for your main party and your reserves, as well as for the other monster wranglers who fight alongside you. ■ An All-New Roguelike Mode for Extended Replayability! Progress even further through the story and a new challenge will unlock in the Battle Arena called the “Wrangler’s Gauntlet” that will truly test your ability as a monster wrangler! Devised by Scruffy, the Wrangler’s Gauntlet provides you with a selection of monsters that changes each time you attempt the challenge. You must use what you’re given to build a party capable of winning 50 consecutive battles. The monsters you befriend here, and the items you obtain, can’t be taken out on your adventures, but with different starting monsters each time and opponents that change with every new attempt, no two runs are ever the same. The roguelike elements offer a fresh perspective on monster wrangling! —The challenge begins once you receive your monsters from Scruffy. He’ll even tell you which monsters you’ll face off against in the next battle, meaning you can tailor your party to best deal with each different opponent. —After winning a battle, you’ll have the opportunity to strengthen your party. sources.name: Gematsu
sources.title: Dementium II coming to Steam on October 20
sources.text: Atooi will release horror first-person shooter sequel Dementium II for PC via Steam on October 20, the developer announced. Dementium II first launched for DS on May 4, 2010, followed by PC on December 17, 2013. The Steam release is a new, “remastered” version. Here is an overview of the game, via its Steam page : The DS horror sequel, reborn. William Redmoor wakes with fresh staples in his skull, inside an institution for the criminally insane, where the walls keep peeling back to expose something worse. Fight, solve, and survive your way out. The cult classic, remastered. The last thing William Redmoor remembers is the Doctor’s scalpel. Now he wakes at the Bright Dawn Treatment Center with a new wound and an old accusation: the records say he murdered his wife. In his cell, a postcard is waiting. The handwriting is his own. It tells him to run. The staff insist he’s recovering. But since the surgery, reality has started to split, and the “hospital” keeps tearing open into a demented version of itself. The Doctor has a theory about why: whatever was wrong inside your head, we let it out! Escaping Bright Dawn is only the beginning. Outside lies an empty village and a countryside crawling with things that shouldn’t exist. Letters signed by his wife lead him deeper. She says she’s waiting for him. Faithful to the Original. Rebuilt for Today You don’t need to have played the first game to survive this one. Here’s what you need to know. In Dementium: The Ward , William Redmoor woke up in a hospital with no memory, surrounded by creatures that had no business being alive. Newspaper clippings claimed he had murdered his wife. Visions of his daughter led him deeper into the dark, while a man in black who called himself the Doctor watched every step. William fought his way down to the basement to face him. It didn’t end the way he hoped. Dementium II begins where that ending left him: under the Doctor’s knife.

sources.name: Eurogamer
sources.title: Fortnite is coming to Linux so we may soon be able to play it and other games like Apex Legends on Steam Deck and Steam Machine
sources.text: Epic Games is officially working on bringing its battle royale shooter Fortnite to Linux. The announcement was tucked away at the bottom of Epic's widely mocked blog post revealing the new, "vibe-coded" Epic Games Store, which is also coming to Linux. At the time, Epic explained it's going to be working with Linux distro maintainers on a set of security requirements needed to run Fortnite. Distros - short for distributions - are operating system variants of Linux, each with its own goals and prioritised system operations. Valve's SteamOS, for instance, is based on Arch Linux. Because of the many discrepancies between Linux distros, each would need to implement Epic's security requirements individually if they want Fortnite to run on their operating system. Fortnite will arrive on Linux via the EGS launcher, but only if a "critical mass of distro maintainers" is reached. Epic didn't specify numbers. This is big news for several reasons. For one, the move would likely make Fortnite playable on SteamOS PCs and handhelds, including Steam Machine and Steam Deck. Furthermore, even if that "critical mass" is never reached, Epic says its work will be available to other developers interested in bringing their games to Linux. Perhaps the biggest reason this is a big deal, however, has to do with Easy Anti-Cheat, the Epic-owned anti-cheat service used in Fortnite and dozens of other games - including Dead by Daylight , Rocket League , Apex Legends , and even Elden Ring . While Easy Anti-Cheat does support Linux, including for some of the games just mentioned, many developers choose not to enable it , simply because its "Linux implementation couldn't offer the same level of protection as our Windows implementation," as Epic explained in a separate blog post . This is why many games that use Easy Anti-Cheat aren't playable on Steam Machine or Steam Deck . The post even names Valve specifically, saying the team will "continue its open line of communication" to support Steam hardware devices "to the maximum extent technically possible". Part of the reason Linux has been a difficult problem for anti-cheat makers to solve is the platform's open nature, meaning certain - required - system-level protections are not guaranteed. On Windows, you can ask users to enable features like TPM 2.0 and Secure Boot , which create that secure environment once hardware requirements are met. While some of that work can be done on Linux, it requires the interest and participation of distro maintainers. Easy Anti-Cheat plans to use Linux features such as signed kernel, signed kernel modules, and secure boot with attestation to achieve that goal. "These requirements build on work that distribution maintainers already do," explains Epic, "and the more distributions that meet these requirements by default, the fewer players will need to change their setup to play." The goal is to "bring the level of protection much closer to par with Windows". There is no timeline for any of this at present, but Easy Anti-Cheat will test the announced plans in Fortnite first before making them available to other developers. In other words, if Fortnite gets a release date on Linux, you'll know the work has paid off and we're closer than ever to achieving anti-cheat parity between Windows and Linux.

sources.title: Toxic Crusaders ‘Gameplay’ trailer
sources.text: Retroware has released a new gameplay trailer for side-scrolling beat ’em up game Toxic Crusaders . Here is an overview of the game, via its Steam page : When the evil Dr. Killemoff attacks, only one team of hideously deformed creatures of superhuman size and strength stands between him and his plans for global pollution: the Toxic Crusaders, earth’s last, greatest and ugliest hope for survival! The hottest heroes of 1991 return for a radical, radioactive beat ’em up for a new era, featuring awesome action, crushing combos and more toxic waste than you’ll know what to do with! Choose from seven playable characters, including Toxie, No-Zone, Junkyard, Major Disaster and Headbanger (who would technically count as two characters if they could only agree on something)—plus, for the first time, play as Toxie’s musically “gifted” girlfriend Yvonne, and the mother of all mothers, Mrs. Junko, Toxie’s mom! Battle across seven disgusting levels rendered in beautiful full-color pixel art as you defend Tromaville from hordes of Radiation Rangers, mutated thugs and zombie chickens. The odds might be stacked against you but with awesome powers, a winning personality and up to four-player local co-up on your side, the Smogulan Empire’s days are numbered! Take a deep breath and dive deep into an action-packed, pun-filled adventure that drags you kicking and screaming through the wonderful world of Troma. Enjoy cameos from gore-filled classics such as Class of Nuke ‘Em High, Poultrygeist: Night of the Chicken Dead, and Sgt. Kabukiman N.Y.P.D.—reimagined in the Saturday morning cartoon style that made this franchise so unforgettable! Toxic Crusaders is due out for PlayStation 5 , Xbox Series , PlayStation 4 , Xbox One , Switch , and PC via Steam in 2026.

sources.title: Heavy Metal Death Can now available for PS5, Xbox Series
sources.text: Survival horror game Heavy Metal Death Can is now available for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series for $17.49, developer Krufs Productions announced. Heavy Metal Death Can first launched for PC via Steam on May 28. Here is an overview of the game, via its Steam page : Heavy Metal Death Can is an old-school survival horror game set on a Swedish Cold War–era submarine. Trapped beneath the ocean, you must fight against the terrifying Sludge which has turned your crew into Zombies. Look for survivors and uncover the truth behind the madness. Classic Survival Horror Emerges from the Depths Heavy Metal Death Can is a retro-inspired survival horror game set on a submarine in an alternate history version of late 70s Sweden. Trapped in the depths of the Norwegian Sea you must fight for survival against the terrifying Sludge which has possessed your crew mates and turned them into horrific zombies. Look for survivors and uncover the truth behind the madness. Step into a claustrophobic, rust-ridden nightmare inspired by genre-defining classics of the PS1 era. With limited ammo, fixed camera angles, and analog dread, every creak of the hull might be your last. Discover the chilling secrets behind the incident on the vessel HMS Domherren. Each corridor reveals fragments of a buried conspiracy… and something not quite human.

sources.name: GamesIndustry.biz
sources.title: Sega and Creative Assembly remove Total War: Shogun 2 remaster from sale as it "falls short of both your expectations and our own standards"
sources.text: Recently launched title has received overwhelmingly negative reviews on Steam, with players citing AI upscaling and performance issues Sega and Creative Assembly have temporarily withdrawn Total War: Shogun 2 – Complete Edition from sale in response to concerns about AI upscaling and other performance issues. Since its October 13 launch, the remaster has received overwhelmingly negative reviews on Steam. Players have reported that assets such as unit cards and new cutscenes display AI-generated features , including extra fingers and armor merging into characters' bodies. As described on Steam , the "underlying graphics technology has been brought to modern standards to take advantage of new methods in rendering," resulting in improved graphics and textures. In response, both companies issued a joint statement acknowledging that the game "has fallen short of both your expectations and our own standards." "We've seen your feedback, comments, and reviews. We agree that the current experience is not where it needs to be." "As a result we are working with platform holders to temporarily remove the game from sale and to reinstate the original game while we investigate the issues. Existing owners will still be able to access and play the game." "We are working closely with our development partner to identify the causes of these problems, deliver improvements, and ensure Shogun 2 – Complete Edition meets the quality standards players expect from Total War." Earlier this year, Sega faced criticism for its use of generative AI in Crazy Taxi: World Tour. The game's Steam page included a generative AI disclaimer, which clarified that Sega uses the technology "as a support tool for developers, aiming to provide better content to our users and enable developers to focus more on creative tasks." "We have used such generative AI support tools during development of Crazy Taxi: World Tour. No AI was used in reference to the performers in game." In a statement to Game Informer , Sega clarified that generative AI was "used to support our teams during the development of background assets" and that "assets generated were still subject to review by the development team."

sources.name: The Verge Games
sources.title: Sega pulls Total War: Shogun 2 remaster from sale following disastrous launch
sources.text: Total War: Shogun 2 — Complete Edition is being removed after users discovered bugs and upscaling that appears to have been done by AI. Total War: Shogun 2 — Complete Edition is being removed after users discovered bugs and upscaling that appears to have been done by AI. If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement. Sega is removing Total War: Shogun 2 — Complete Edition from storefronts following a disastrous launch where users complained about issues like bugs and upscaling that appears to have been done by AI. Complete Edition , a remaster of the 2011 strategy game, launched on Tuesday, and it bundled the main game and all of its DLC with promised upgrades including “improved visuals,” “1440p and 4K UI scaling,” and modernized controls. It has an “Overwhelmingly Negative” rating on Steam , where it has already been pulled, and posts on Reddit showcase artwork that users believe AI messed up. “We’re aware that Total War: Shogun 2 – Complete Edition has fallen short of both your expectations and our own standards,” Sega and developer Creative Assembly wrote in a post . “We’ve seen your feedback, comments, and reviews. We agree that the current experience is not where it needs to be.” The two companies say they will “reinstate the original game,” and existing owners will “still be able to access ” Complete Edition . Sega and Creative Assembly say that they are “working closely with our development partner to identify the causes of these problems, deliver improvements, and ensure Shogun 2 - Complete Edition meets the quality standards players expect from Total War.” A studio called Mataboo is also listed as a developer for the game on Steam, and Mataboo highlights its work on the game on its website .

stories.title: I Never Played Ocarina of Time, But 2 Hours With the Remake Proves There’s So Much More to This Masterpiece Than Nostalgia
stories.summary: I never played Ocarina of Time, but 2 hours with the remake proves there’s so much more to this masterpiece than nostalgia.

sources.name: IGN
sources.title: I Never Played Ocarina of Time, But 2 Hours With the Remake Proves There’s So Much More to This Masterpiece Than Nostalgia
sources.text: No matter how much I wish it were the case, I’ll never know what it was like to have seen Jaws in the summer of 1975. Yet, I still get the joy of watching the film that changed blockbuster cinema forever 50 years later, whether that be on towering IMAX screens or wonderfully restored 4K blu-rays. The experience of being there when a film, game, or piece of music entered our culture and witnessing its impact firsthand can never be replicated, but through preservation, remasters, and remakes, new audiences get to uncover these treasures for themselves. This is the case with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. My recent playtime with a demo of the Switch 2 remake felt like digital archaeology; the unearthing of a cultural artefact that informed so much of what came after it, while remaining a gleaming treasure in its own right. A link between one era of video games and another. A sacred text. At least, that’s how it felt to me. You see, I’ve never played the original. Well, that’s a tiny bit of a lie — I did briefly mess around in the opening hour or so of the 3DS port around a decade ago. I know, I should be subject to whatever form of medieval torture you deem appropriate. But the truth is, it’s one that simply passed me by, despite having played several Zeldas since — Tears of the Kingdom is a masterwork of open-world design in my eyes, even if Wind Waker still sits closest to my heart. I never owned a Nintendo 64, and likely got distracted by whatever was happening in my mid-20s, which made me put down Ocarina’s portable version. But now, finally, I’m ready to right my wrongs, and after playing two hours of the remake, I couldn’t be more excited to do so. During my time with the 2026 version of Link’s most defining adventure, I got to play through Kokiri Forest, wander around Castle Town, and complete the Forest Temple. Even from this small sample size, I could see flashes of some of my favourite games within it, and the inspirational sparks it must have fired off into other game developers' minds in 1998. But most importantly, I had a ridiculously fun time with it. From just that short session, I can safely assure you that, if you’re like me and have also somehow let this piece of history slip through your fingers, there’s plenty here for newcomers to enjoy. When it launches in November, there will be little excuse to leave it unplayed. “Anyone who makes 3D games who says they’ve not borrowed something from Mario or Zelda is lying — from the games on Nintendo 64, not necessarily the ones from today,” said Rockstar co-founder Dan Houser to the New York Times . It’s a point that’s hard to argue with, and one I wouldn’t dare contest — I think one of the minds behind GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2 probably knows more about game design than I. Nintendo having created something of a lending library for game design is something I could see most clearly in the Forest Temple. I enjoyed unpicking each of its knotted series of corridors and unpacking its hidden secrets, all wrapped in a spooky mansion setting. Every room is a puzzle, whether in the more traditional sense of moving heavy stone cubes around to unblock routes or navigating combat challenges that put your tool belt to the test. Battles are never overly challenging but wonderfully engaging, with looming sword-and-shield-wielding skeletons reacting to your actions as you, in turn, have to counter theirs with a well-timed dodge or stun. When striking them down, you can see the basic structure that would go on to influence Batman Arkham’s brawls — one of the defining melee combat systems — in the way that fights carry the rhythm of enemies reading your movements and you, in turn, having to react with the correct rock-paper-scissors response. Outside of scraps, the structure of the whole temple can’t help but conjure memories of Dark Souls' intertwining, shortcut-unlocking approach to level design. Every route loops back to its central chamber, in which four coloured flames need to be lit in order for the path to the boss to reveal itself. The construction of this area is masterfully done, clearly indicating what you have to achieve without ever holding your hand too much. That freedom of thought has always been prevalent in Zelda, all the way up to how Tears of the Kingdom brings out your most experimental thoughts with its building systems. In Ocarina, breadcrumbs of clues as to how to achieve objectives are given, with tempting buttons placed out of reach behind locked gates and high up ledges seemingly unreachable. That’s until you realise you can rotate the hallways and alter the architecture of the temple completely, like some sort of prototype of Dishonored 2’s Clockwork Mansion. This mechanic is key to navigating the space, and where much of its challenge lies. Entire projects, such as Fez, have gone on to use a system like this to power a whole game. Here, it’s utilised for less than an hour. It’s a testament to the enduring inventiveness of Nintendo that these ideas still echo through gaming today. I found great joy in the simplicity of the temple, but one that tickled my brain enough to never seem like child’s play. There’s a delicate balance when it comes to signposting without holding your hand, to the point where the temple delivered several “aha” moments over the course of my time exploring it. Some came naturally through decades of playing video games, like seeing a frozen target with a raging fire nearby, clearly indicating I needed to fire an arrow through the flames to melt it. But some did give me pause for thought, such as not realising I needed to use my bow to knock each of the temple’s four guardian sprites out of paintings in order to progress. Still, I tried it anyway, and lo and behold, it worked. It’s that sort of “let's see if this works” experimentation that I’ve always appreciated in Zelda, so it’s no surprise to see it pioneered here in the series first foray into 3D. sources.text: Previews indicate Nintendo really cares about this one Switchboard is Polygon's weekly newsletter for all things Nintendo, sent on Thursdays and published on the site on Saturdays. You can subscribe here . Guess what — Nintendo's all-in on physical media. This unsurprising fact became news this week after an executive for Nintendo in Latin America made some mild and extremely uncontroversial comments to the effect. "We know how much the fans like it," Bill van Zyll said, while pointing out that the company had just launched a new platform, in Switch 2, that supports physical cartridges. This is only worth noting due to Sony's unpopular decision to end production of physical PlayStation games starting in 2028, but still: good to know. As a family-oriented company which still has strong ties to toy retail, Nintendo enjoys a far higher proportion of physical retail sales than any of its competitors, so this position just makes a boring kind of sense. But it also has more to lose; as pressure on memory chip prices continues, Switch game cards are surely much more expensive to manufacture than Blu-ray discs. Hence the functionally empty game-key cards most third-party publishers have resorted to. But when it comes to its own titles, Nintendo still insists on shipping the full game on the card, and hang the expense. You can tell what matters to Nintendo by what it chooses to spend money on. It typically doesn't go overboard on development budgets for its games, reasoning that expensive graphical fidelity won't add a proportional amount of fun. (It would also take up more of those costly gigabytes). But Nintendo goes out of pocket to put all of, say, next month's Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on a game card, because it is a proportionally better experience. Imagine being nine years old, unwrapping the game for Christmas, putting it in your Switch 2 and then having to wait for it to download. Unacceptable. First hands-on impressions of the Ocarina remake were published this week, and Polygon's Michael McWhertor found it "snappy, streamlined, and polished in ways that make it feel totally fresh." Here again, Nintendo's priorities are instructive. Nintendo has revisited this game several times before, but this time is different. The 3DS' Ocarina of Time 3D was handed to an external team, Grezzo, as was the pretty but laggy 2019 remake of Link's Awakening . But Ocarina 2026, unlike its sister N64-era remake Star Fox , appears to have been allocated to one of Nintendo's precious internal teams, and the difference is apparent. Beyond the lush visuals, previewers all noted how frictionless and responsive the remake is, a huge correction of the biggest historical flaw with one of Nintendo's greatest games. (The original N64 game runs at a sluggish 20 frames per second, and you can really feel it.) Nintendo has the same cynical reasons for leaning on remakes to pad out the release schedule as every other publisher. Games are risky endeavors, and new ideas are hard to come by. But in this case, it seems Nintendo also saw an opportunity to make a classic game meaningfully better, and — just as with its first-party game cards — refused to take half measures. This is about legacy, about brand reputation. And there's little Nintendo cares about more. The PlayStation Portable cult classic Patapon , a rhythm-action game about a line of little marching warriors, has been reimagined by some of its original developers in a roguelike spiritual sequel. It doesn't quite hang together, but it's a powerful nostalgia trip all the same. As the excellent Castlevania: Belmont's Curse arrives on Switch, it's a good moment to revisit this half-forgotten Sega Genesis entry in the series. It's not the Castlevania you know; instead, it's a perfect, technologically impressive expression of a more straight-ahead action game like the NES originals. The strange, funhouse-mirror atmosphere of Ocarina of Time 's direct sequel is captured perfectly by this carnivalesque retread of the "Song of Storms" melody, as if performed by a circus organ-grinder and their monkey. stories.title: Joguei o remake de Zelda: Ocarina of Time e o clássico envelheceu bem
stories.summary: Após 90 minutos de demo, o remake chega ao Switch 2 em 5 de novembro com visual refeito, dublagem em português e ocarina que reconhece a voz. O post Joguei o remake de Zelda: Ocarina of Time e o clássico envelheceu bem apareceu primeiro em Olhar Digital .

sources.name: Olhar Digital Games
sources.title: Joguei o remake de Zelda: Ocarina of Time e o clássico envelheceu bem
sources.text: O remake de The Legend of Zelda : Ocarina of Time chega ao Nintendo Switch 2 em 5 de novembro de 2026. Ele mantém a estrutura do clássico de 1998, mas muda o jeito de ver e de jogar. Joguei cerca de 90 minutos, e a primeira impressão é de um jogo que não parece velho nem desatualizado. Como estreante em Ocarina of Time, achei o desafio alto. Já joguei Zelda II: The Adventure of Link no NES, mas nunca Ocarina of Time. Por isso, este texto traz o olhar de quem chega sem nostalgia e evita spoilers, mesmo os que não surpreenderiam quem já jogou. As comparações com o original vêm de colegas que conhecem o jogo e testaram a mesma demonstração. O Olhar Digital foi convidado para jogar em primeira mão, e fui ao México viver esta experiência com outros influenciadores e pessoas da imprensa. Jogamos três partes diferentes, escolhidas para mostrar momentos, itens e mecânicas variadas. Primeiro veio o começo na Floresta Kokiri. Depois, uma exploração pelo Campo de Hyrule e pela Cidade do Castelo. Por fim, o Templo da Floresta, onde confesso que travei. Lançado originalmente para o Nintendo 64 em 1998, Ocarina of Time ganhou um primeiro remake no Nintendo 3DS, em 2011. O remake de Zelda: Ocarina of Time é exclusivo do Switch 2 e aparece em um ano simbólico, o dos 40 anos da série. Na loja oficial da Nintendo do Brasil, o jogo custa R$ 329,90 na versão digital e ocupa cerca de 27 GB. Ele pode ser jogado no modo TV, semiportátil ou portátil, e já chega com texto e dublagem em português do Brasil. Quem já jogou outros exclusivos de lançamento da Nintendo, como Mario Kart World, sabe que o Switch 2 tem processamento de sobra. Em Zelda isso não mudou: a qualidade gráfica está linda. Segundo colegas que conhecem o original, os detalhes dos personagens estão fiéis ao jogo de 1998, com um toque a mais de modernidade. Joguei na TV, e as cutscenes são fluidas e encantadoras. O que mais me impressionou foi o conjunto: a arte gráfica, a dublagem em português e a trilha sonora trabalham juntas e transportam você para dentro do jogo. Em uma cena, a Grande Árvore Deko pede à Navi que procure o Link. Dá para sentir o peso da voz de Deko, a pressa da fada e o clima de expectativa. É meio que só assistindo mesmo para sentir, mas foi bem imersivo. Como já saiu um trailer com mais detalhes, dá para ver o cenário e as peças de roupa nítidos, rodando a 60 FPS. A Nintendo não divulgou números oficiais de resolução e taxa de quadros do jogo, e a página da loja no Brasil também não traz esses dados. Na TV, o que vi foi movimento e cenas fluidas. Os comandos de Link são simples: corrida, pulo e mira por giroscópio nas armas de projétil, como o estilingue. Quem conhece o original vai notar o botão de pulo, já que antes Link pulava sozinho nas bordas, e a câmera livre. As duas mudanças foram anunciadas pela Nintendo. O combate tem impacto sonoro e visual forte. Dá para pedir ajuda à Navi em várias situações, na qual ela explica os pontos fracos dos monstros, e colegas que conhecem o original disseram que ela está menos intrusiva do que no jogo de 1998. Esse recurso auxilia para não travar em certos momentos: não se esqueça de usá-lo! Joguei com pro controller, e não com Joy-Con, que, pelo que me disseram, também deve ser tranquilo. Na hora de trazer o review completo, conto como foi a experiência no modo portátil. A primeira parte foi o tutorial na Floresta Kokiri. Link precisa buscar os primeiros itens para encontrar a Grande Árvore Deko e iniciar a aventura, e Mido o impede de passar enquanto ele não tiver espada e escudo. Quem já conhece o jogo vai direto para os desafios. Por causa do tempo, fiquei com receio de explorar demais e perder as outras partes. Não conversei com todo mundo da vila e fui mais objetiva, até porque passei pelo tutorial para aprender os movimentos básicos. Depois da árvore, Link é enviado para sua aventura na floresta. Ali enfrentei as primeiras plantas carnívoras e, no meu caso, levei susto com aranhas gigantes que caem do teto da caverna. Há outros itens iniciais por lá, mas o mais importante foi encontrar o estilingue. Um aviso para quem tem aracnofobia, como eu: nessa fase há muitas aranhas. Não procurei nas opções para mudá-las, mas, como são fantasiosas, consegui me controlar. O Campo de Hyrule foi um momento de exploração, mas, por causa do tempo, fiz pouco. O campo é grande, e eu quis conhecer mais a Cidade do Castelo de Hyrule do que o campo em si. A cidade é linda, com pessoas interagindo, e os detalhes parecem de filme. Entrei em algumas lojinhas, mas me dediquei mais à missão da loja de insetos. A última parte foi o Templo da Floresta. Nessa dungeon há diversas salas, cada uma com um puzzle diferente para resolver, o que leva à parte seguinte. São quatro portas, e eu consegui resolver uma e meia, rs. A primeira é a mais simples. Depois, se você não acertar a ordem de resolução das coisas, isso te trava. Os puzzles são desafiadores e interessantes: envolvem mover blocos de área, acertar lugares estratégicos, coletar chaves pequenas e explorar corredores, como em um calabouço clássico. É por isso que digo que o jogo envelheceu bem e traz de volta o desafio dos jogos antigos. Na minha opinião, o desafio mais encantador é usar a ocarina. Você pode cantar para o console, murmurar ou até usar um instrumento para reproduzir a canção. O microfone do Switch 2 capta o som, identifica a melodia e reconhece a música, e Link a toca no jogo. Segundo a Nintendo, no remake de Zelda: Ocarina of Time funcionam as canções que Link já aprendeu, e os botões continuam disponíveis. O recurso foi demonstrado pelo produtor Eiji Aonuma em um Nintendo Direct. No meu ponto de vista, ele deixa o jogo mais dinâmico. Muita gente tem dificuldade com ritmo no controle, e talvez cantarolar fique mais fácil. Também estão previstas para este ano ocarinas oficiais, incluindo um modelo elétrico da HORI. A dublagem em português ficou incrível: bem adaptada e acessível, e dá para perceber a preocupação da equipe da Nintendo com

sources.title: Zelda Ocarina of Time remake has new sidequests, harder minigames, and subtle dungeon tweaks
sources.text: Maybe there are a few surprises to be found after all I can't help but feel Nintendo is being a little too faithful with its upcoming The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake . I know I'm pretty isolated in that opinion, but with new info coming out of recent hands-on previews of the game, I've suddenly got reason to believe that Nintendo is looking out for my tastes, too. The Ocarina of Time remake will feature some new side quests, as demonstrated by longtime Zelda YouTube Zeltik . In Hyrule Castle Town, the guy at the potion shop will now be freaking out about a lurking bug when you first meet him, handing over an empty bottle for Link to catch it. Fulfill his request, and he'll let you keep the bottle and offer to fill it up with a healing red potion. This certainly isn't the kind of multi-stage side quest that you'd expect to have in a modern action-adventure game – and certainly, it doesn't seem that there's a journal or anything where you can track side missions – but it does suggest that Nintendo has designs on offering some things to do that'll be fresh even for those of us who've played through Ocarina of Time a dozen times over. There's also a new, harder version of the target shooting game where you have much less time to hit the targets, suggesting that we can expect some new challenge levels in the minigames, too. Zeltik's video also goes into depth on some minor, but meaningful, tweaks to the layout of the Forest Temple, suggesting that we won't be sleepwalking through the old dungeons, either. I was ten years old when I first played Ocarina of Time on N64, and it set me on a path to loving video games so much that they'd eventually become my job. I should be the perfect audience for the remake, but I've honestly been a little disappointed with how safe Nintendo seemed to be playing it. I know, I know, you can't mess too much with a stone-cold classic, but I already know Ocarina of Time forward and backward, and I'm afraid trundling through a remake offering little more than prettier graphics would ultimately feel a little empty. Offering a few little surprises around the edges, though? That suddenly makes the prospect of revisiting Hyrule a lot more exciting. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's Hyrule feels more alive than ever thanks to clever expansion and a dose of Breath of the Wild vibes. Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week Dustin Bailey joined the GamesRadar team as a Staff Writer in May 2022, and is currently based in Missouri. He's been covering games (with occasional dalliances in the worlds of anime and pro wrestling) since 2015, first as a freelancer, then as a news writer at PCGamesN for nearly five years. His love for games was sparked somewhere between Metal Gear Solid 2 and Knights of the Old Republic, and these days you can usually find him splitting his entertainment time between retro gaming, the latest big action-adventure title, or a long haul in American Truck Simulator.
